_link.title: I can identify which aspects of collision theory are affected by a change in surface area

toLevel2.stem: Which aspect of collision theory is affected by increasing the surface area of a solid reactant?
distractors: Collision energy
Particle orientation
Activation energy

toLevel2.stem: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant does NOT affect:
distractors: How often particles collide
The frequency of collisions per second
The number of exposed particles

toLevel2.stem: Why does breaking a solid into smaller pieces increase reaction rate?
toLevel2.answer: More particles are exposed and available to collide
distractors: Each particle gains more kinetic energy
The activation energy is reduced
The particles align in better orientations

toLevel2.stem: Increasing the surface area of a reactant increases:
toLevel2.answer: the number of particles accessible for collisions
distractors: the kinetic energy of each particle
the proportion of particles exceeding Ea
the orientation of colliding particles

toLevel2.stem: Does changing the surface area of a solid affect the orientation of particle collisions?
distractors: Yes, it improves orientation
Yes, it worsens orientation
Yes, it eliminates the orientation requirement

toLevel2.stem: Increasing surface area increases the frequency of collisions between reactant particles.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Crushing a solid into a powder increases the kinetic energy of the individual particles.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: Increasing surface area increases collision {{blank:1}} but does not change the {{blank:2}} of individual collisions.
distractors: energy

distractors: products

distractors: hidden

toLevel3.stem: Why doesn't increasing surface area change the kinetic energy of individual particles?
toLevel3.answer: Kinetic energy depends on temperature, not on how many particles are exposed
distractors: Smaller pieces always have less energy than larger pieces of the same substance
Surface area and kinetic energy are measured in the same units
Kinetic energy only changes when a catalyst is added to the reaction

toLevel3.stem: How does surface area differ from temperature in its effect on collision theory?
toLevel3.answer: Surface area affects frequency only; temperature affects both frequency and energy
distractors: Surface area affects energy only; temperature affects frequency only
Both affect collision frequency and energy in exactly the same way
Surface area affects orientation; temperature affects frequency only

toLevel3.stem: A large block of zinc is cut into small cubes. What happens to the total number of zinc atoms?
toLevel3.answer: It stays the same — only the number of exposed atoms increases
distractors: It increases because cutting creates new atoms from the zinc
It decreases because some atoms are lost during cutting
It doubles each time the block is cut in half

toLevel3.stem: Why is surface area particularly relevant for reactions involving solids?
toLevel3.answer: Only particles on the surface of a solid are available to collide with the other reactant
distractors: Solid particles have lower kinetic energy than liquid or gas particles
Solids cannot react unless they are first dissolved in a solution
Surface area affects the activation energy of reactions with solids

toLevel3.stem: A student says: 'Grinding a solid into powder makes each particle collide harder.' Why is this incorrect?
toLevel3.answer: Grinding exposes more particles but does not increase the energy of each collision
distractors: Grinding does make particles collide harder because they are smaller
Grinding reduces the energy of collisions because particles are lighter
Grinding changes the orientation of particles, not their collision energy

toLevel3.stem: How does surface area relate to the concept of 'accessibility' in collision theory?
toLevel3.answer: Greater surface area means more reactant particles are accessible for collisions
distractors: Greater surface area means particles need less energy to react
Greater surface area makes particles orient correctly more often
Greater surface area reduces the number of accessible particles

toLevel3.stem: Surface area affects collision frequency because it determines how many solid particles are exposed to the other reactant.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Surface area affects only collision {{blank:1}}, while temperature affects both frequency and {{blank:2}}.
distractors: energy
orientation
orientation
frequency

toLevel3.stem: Only particles on the {{blank:1}} of a solid are available to {{blank:2}} with the other reactant.
distractors: inside
dissolve
edge

toLevel3.stem: Grinding a solid into powder does not increase the {{blank:1}} of each collision — it only exposes more {{blank:2}} for reaction.
distractors: frequency
catalysts
orientation
products

toLevel4.stem: A student reacts a whole block of calcium carbonate with HCl in one trial and the same mass of powdered calcium carbonate in another. Both trials are at the same temperature. Which trial is faster and why?
toLevel4.answer: The powdered trial is faster because more CaCO₃ particles are exposed for collisions
distractors: The block trial is faster because the block has more total particles
Both trials are the same speed because the mass and temperature are identical
The powdered trial is faster because each particle has more kinetic energy

toLevel4.stem: A student writes: 'Crushing the marble chips increased the rate because each chip now has more energy.' What correction is needed?
toLevel4.answer: Crushing exposed more particles for collisions; the energy per particle is unchanged
distractors: The explanation is correct — smaller chips have more energy per particle
Crushing reduced the activation energy, which is why the rate increased
Crushing improved the orientation of collisions, not the energy

toLevel4.stem: Iron filings react with oxygen much faster than an iron nail of the same mass. Using collision theory, which factor explains this?
toLevel4.answer: Iron filings have a much greater surface area, increasing collision frequency
distractors: Iron filings have higher kinetic energy than an iron nail
Iron filings have a lower activation energy than an iron nail
Iron filings have better particle orientation than an iron nail

toLevel4.stem: A student investigates the effect of surface area on the reaction between zinc and sulfuric acid. They use zinc granules in one trial and zinc powder in another. What variable must they keep constant?
toLevel4.answer: The mass of zinc and the concentration and temperature of the acid
distractors: The surface area of zinc and the volume of the acid used
The size of zinc pieces and the concentration of the acid
Only the temperature needs to be constant, nothing else

toLevel4.stem: Grain dust in silos can cause explosions. Using collision theory, why is fine dust more dangerous than whole grains?
toLevel4.answer: Fine dust has much greater surface area, massively increasing collision frequency with oxygen
distractors: Fine dust has higher kinetic energy than whole grains of the same material
Fine dust lowers the activation energy of the combustion reaction
Fine dust aligns better with oxygen molecules for correct orientation

toLevel4.stem: A student wants to slow down a reaction between a metal and an acid without changing temperature or concentration. What should they do?
toLevel4.answer: Use a larger piece of metal with less surface area exposed
distractors: Grind the metal into a fine powder to spread it out
Add a catalyst to provide an alternative reaction pathway
Use a different acid with the same concentration

toLevel4.stem: A student compares the effects of surface area and concentration on rate. Both increase rate. What do they have in common in terms of collision theory?
toLevel4.answer: Both increase collision frequency without changing collision energy
distractors: Both increase collision energy without changing collision frequency
Both lower the activation energy of the reaction equally
Both improve the orientation of particles during collisions

toLevel4.stem: Iron filings react faster than an iron nail because the filings have a greater {{blank:1}} area, which increases collision {{blank:2}}.
distractors: cross-sectional
energy
total
orientation

toLevel4.stem: Grain dust is dangerous in silos because the fine particles have a very large {{blank:1}} area, leading to extremely rapid {{blank:2}} with oxygen.
distractors: cross-sectional
decomposition
internal
evaporation

toLevel4.stem: To slow a reaction with a metal, a student should use a {{blank:1}} piece rather than a powder, because this reduces the number of {{blank:2}} particles.
distractors: smaller
energetic
hotter
oriented

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that surface area and temperature both affect the same collision theory factors. Analyze this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — surface area affects frequency only, while temperature affects both frequency and energy
distractors: Correct — both affect collision frequency and collision energy equally
Incorrect — surface area affects energy only, while temperature affects frequency
Correct — both affect only collision frequency through identical mechanisms

toLevel5.stem: A reaction between a solid and an acid is very slow even when the solid is finely ground. What other collision theory factor might explain the slow rate?
toLevel5.answer: The reaction may have a high activation energy, so few collisions are energetic enough
distractors: The solid must be ground even finer until atoms are individually separated
The acid concentration must be zero for the reaction to proceed
Surface area is the only factor that affects rate for solid-acid reactions

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Since both surface area and concentration affect only collision frequency, their effects on rate must be identical.' Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: They affect frequency by different mechanisms — one exposes particles, the other packs more into a volume
distractors: The reasoning is correct — both factors are completely interchangeable
The reasoning is flawed because concentration also affects collision energy
The reasoning is flawed because surface area also affects activation energy

toLevel5.stem: Would increasing the surface area of a solid reactant affect the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve in any way?
toLevel5.answer: No — the curve depends on temperature, which surface area does not change
distractors: Yes — the curve would shift right because more particles are exposed
Yes — the curve would become taller because more particles are involved
Yes — the Ea line would move left because surface area lowers Ea

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'In a reaction between two aqueous solutions, increasing surface area would increase the rate.' Is this valid?
toLevel5.answer: No — surface area is relevant for solid reactants, not dissolved species already dispersed in solution
distractors: Yes — surface area always affects rate regardless of the state of the reactants
Yes — aqueous solutions have surfaces that can be increased by stirring
No — surface area never affects rate for any type of reaction

toLevel5.stem: In an explosion, a fine metal dust reacts almost instantaneously with oxygen. A block of the same metal barely reacts. What collision theory analysis explains this extreme difference?
toLevel5.answer: The dust has enormously greater surface area, creating vastly more simultaneous collisions with O₂
distractors: The dust has a much lower activation energy than the metal block
The dust particles have much higher kinetic energy than the block particles
The dust particles orient themselves perfectly while block particles cannot

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that grinding a solid catalyst into a powder would make it more effective. Using collision theory, is this suggestion reasonable?
toLevel5.answer: Yes — more surface area means more reactant particles can access the catalytic surface
distractors: No — catalysts work by lowering Ea, which is unrelated to surface area
No — grinding a catalyst would destroy its catalytic properties entirely
Yes — but only because grinding increases the kinetic energy of the catalyst

toLevel5.stem: A reaction between solid A and solution B is run with large chunks of A, then repeated with fine powder of A. The temperature and concentration are identical. The powder reacts 20 times faster. What does this tell us?
toLevel5.answer: The powder has approximately 20 times more surface area, giving 20 times more collision opportunities
distractors: The powder has 20 times more kinetic energy per particle than the chunks
The activation energy decreased by a factor of 20 when powder was used
The powder particles orient 20 times better than the chunk particles

distractors: solid
separated
gaseous
compressed

toLevel5.stem: Surface area and concentration both increase collision {{blank:1}} but by different mechanisms: surface area exposes more particles, while concentration packs more into a given {{blank:2}}.
